title: Distributed SQL and NewSQL
problem: One PostgreSQL primary has run out of write capacity and disk, and sharding it by hand would break the transactions and joins the product depends on.
summary: Distributed SQL databases such as Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB split tables into key ranges, replicate each range with Raft or Paxos, run two-phase commit across ranges and order commits with a clock service, so one SQL endpoint survives node and region loss.
catTip: I used to nap on one big database server. Now the humans spread my bed across three towns and only count me asleep once two of the three beds agree. Very safe. Also slower to lie down, every single time.

recall.q: What does a distributed SQL database do that sharded PostgreSQL cannot, and what does every write pay for it?
recall.a: It splits tables into ranges it moves itself, replicates each range with Raft or Paxos, and runs two-phase commit across ranges so cross-shard transactions are ordinary. Every write pays at least one consensus round trip, which across regions is the round trip to the nearest other region.

guide.breaks: A single primary caps write throughput and loses acknowledged writes on failover, while hand-sharding behind a router leaves cross-shard transactions, unique constraints and joins to the application.
guide.tradeoffs: Every write waits for a consensus majority, so latency rises with the distance between replicas, sequential keys create hot ranges, and the cluster needs far more operational care than one server.
guide.explainSimply: Imagine a ledger copied to three towns, where a sale only counts once two of the three clerks have initialled it and a town-hall clock stamps the order of entries. Nothing is lost if one town burns down, but every sale takes a little longer. That is distributed SQL.
guide.hint: Think about what replaces the primary, and what every write has to wait for.

meow: Three beds in three towns, meow. I am only officially asleep when two agree. Safe nap, slow nap.

quiz.prompt: A team runs CockroachDB with replicas in Mumbai, Singapore and Frankfurt so that the database survives a region failure. What happens to write latency compared with a single-region cluster?
options: Nothing changes, because Raft commits on the leader and replicates to the other regions asynchronously
Every write waits at least the round trip to the nearest other region, because a majority of replicas must acknowledge it
Only transactions that touch several ranges slow down; a single-row write stays local to its leader's region
Writes get faster, because three regions share the write load
quiz.explanation: A write commits when a majority of its range's replicas have it, and with one replica per region that majority always includes another region. The third option is the tempting error: even a single-row write is a Raft commit that needs that majority, so there is no local fast path.

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes distributed SQL from sharded PostgreSQL behind a router such as Citus?
options: Distributed SQL cannot run joins, because rows live on different machines
Sharded PostgreSQL replicates each shard with consensus, while distributed SQL uses a primary and replicas
Distributed SQL splits and moves key ranges itself, replicates each range by consensus and treats cross-range transactions as ordinary
Sharded PostgreSQL cannot scale writes beyond one machine
quiz.explanation: The difference is where the shard edge lives: distributed SQL puts ranges, consensus and cross-range two-phase commit inside the database. The last option is the strongest distractor because sharding does scale writes; what it cannot do cheaply is a transaction or a constraint that crosses shards.

cards.q: Your orders table on CockroachDB uses an auto-increment primary key and inserts slow down under load. Why, and what would you change?
cards.a: Sequential keys send every insert to the last range, so one leader is the whole cluster's bottleneck. Load-based splitting cannot split a single hot key, so use a random or hash-prefixed key to spread inserts across ranges.

cards.q: What is Spanner's commit wait, and why does CockroachDB not need one?
cards.a: Spanner waits out TrueTime's uncertainty interval before acknowledging a commit so that its timestamp is externally consistent. CockroachDB has no bounded clock; instead a read that meets a write inside its uncertainty window restarts at a later timestamp, paying only on conflict.

glossary.note: A central service that hands out monotonically increasing timestamps to order transactions; in TiDB it is provided by the Placement Driver.

sources.title: Spanner documentation, Replication
sources.supports: splits replicated with Paxos; witness replicas vote but do not serve reads; stale reads served by the closest caught-up replica at 15 seconds or more of staleness

sources.title: Spanner documentation, Life of Spanner reads and writes
sources.supports: two-phase commit across splits with one split's leader as coordinator; commit wait before the outcome is returned

sources.title: Spanner documentation, TrueTime and external consistency (Spanner Omni)
sources.supports: TrueTime represents time as an interval from earliest to latest; higher uncertainty lengthens commit wait

sources.title: Spanner documentation, Reads
sources.supports: strong reads are the default; bounded-staleness and exact-staleness reads; 15 seconds suggested as a reasonable staleness

sources.title: Spanner documentation, Instance configurations
sources.supports: regional configurations hold three read-write replicas in three zones; multi-region configurations add replicas and a witness in other regions

sources.title: Spanner documentation, Transactions
sources.supports: serializable isolation is Spanner's default

sources.title: Corbett et al., "Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database", OSDI 2012, sections 3 and 4
sources.supports: TrueTime built on GPS and atomic clocks; uncertainty a sawtooth of about 1 to 7 ms, 4 ms on average; commit wait

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, Replication Controls (configure replication zones)
sources.supports: range_max_bytes default 512 MiB; num_replicas default 3

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, Distribution Layer
sources.supports: a range that reaches its size limit splits into two, each its own Raft group

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, Transaction Layer
sources.supports: write intents and the transaction record; parallel commits reduce commit from two rounds of consensus to one; hybrid logical clocks; a node crashes when its offset exceeds 80% of the maximum; uncertainty-window read restarts

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, cockroach start (--max-offset)
sources.supports: maximum allowed clock offset defaults to 500ms; servers crash if observed offsets exceed it

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, Transactions
sources.supports: SERIALIZABLE is the default isolation level

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, Follower Reads
sources.supports: follower_read_timestamp() reads data at least 4.2 seconds in the past from the nearest replica

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, Multi-region survival goals
sources.supports: surviving a region failure needs at least three regions and raises write latency by at least the round trip to the nearest region

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, Global tables
sources.supports: global tables serve consistent local reads in every region at the cost of higher write latency from a commit-wait step

sources.title: CockroachDB documentation, Load-based splitting
sources.supports: load-based splitting is on by default with a threshold of 2,500 queries per second

sources.title: TiDB documentation, TiKV configuration file (region-split-size)
sources.supports: Region split size defaults to 256 MiB; before v8.4.0 the default was 96 MiB

sources.title: TiDB documentation, PD configuration file (max-replicas)
sources.supports: three replicas per Region by default

sources.title: TiDB documentation, TSO
sources.supports: PD provides the timestamp oracle whose timestamps always move forward

sources.title: TiDB documentation, TiDB FAQ (transaction model)
sources.supports: TiDB's transaction model is a Percolator-style two-phase commit with PD as the timestamp allocator

sources.title: TiDB documentation, Pessimistic transaction mode
sources.supports: clusters created from v3.0.8 use pessimistic transactions by default

sources.title: TiDB documentation, Follower Read
sources.supports: the tidb_replica_read variable sends reads to follower replicas

sources.title: TiDB documentation, Transaction isolation levels
sources.supports: TiDB implements snapshot isolation and advertises it as REPEATABLE READ for MySQL compatibility

sources.title: Vitess documentation, What is Vitess and History
sources.supports: Vitess was created at YouTube in 2010; VTGate is the proxy that routes MySQL-protocol queries to shards

sources.title: Citus documentation, Concepts
sources.supports: Citus is a PostgreSQL extension with a coordinator and workers; tables are distributed by a distribution column

sources.title: Pavlo and Aslett, "What's Really New with NewSQL?", SIGMOD Record 45(2), 2016
sources.supports: the term NewSQL was first used by Aslett in a 2011 analyst report
